```diff
-#if 0
+// JusPrin: enabled. The header's printer menu reports the machine's live state for print hosts
+// (SetupCommands::printer_connection), which needs the status stream this block starts.
+#if 1
         // Query initial status
```

What that block does is upstream's own code: after connecting, query the printer's status once and open the websocket stream. OrcaSlicer wrote it, then disabled it because their Monitor tab does not show Moonraker printers. JusPrin's printer menu does want that state, so the block is switched on. No upstream line was deleted or rewritten, and the fork now owns a policy ("print hosts report live state") rather than any upstream behavior.

The rebase evidence the fork rules ask for:

- Upstream's current main still has the same comment and `#if 0` at that spot, so a rebase merges this hunk cleanly today. I checked with a merge-tree simulation from the fork base to upstream main; the four pre-existing conflicts on the fork are in other files, none in the files this work touches.
- The day upstream enables the block themselves, the hunk becomes a trivial conflict whose correct resolution is to take upstream's version and drop the JusPrin comment.
- Because the flag sits in the agent and not the shell, there was no fork-owned place to put it. Reimplementing the status stream in the shell would have duplicated about 200 upstream lines, which the stewardship rules rate worse than a two-line switch.

Two things the change does not touch: the SSL-scheme bug in `DevManager.cpp`, which the session you started is handling, and Bambu printers, which take the same path as before.
why is this necessary?

Because the menu's state is computed from data that only that block produces.

The shell derives the row from two questions it asks the machine object. "Is it connected?" is answered by a timestamp: true only if a status message from the printer arrived within the last 30 seconds. "Is it printing?" is answered by the print state carried in the most recent status message. Neither is fetched on demand; both are filled in only when the printer agent pushes a status message into the app.

For Bambu printers those messages arrive over MQTT, so the shell already worked. For Moonraker, the only code that produces them is the status query and websocket loop inside that disabled block. With it off, the agent connects, checks `/server/info` once, and then never sends anything. So the machine object's timestamp never refreshes, and the menu could only ever say "Offline", with the shell change alone. That is what my first test run would have shown had I not enabled it.

The alternatives were worse:

- Have the shell talk HTTP to the printer itself. Wrong layer, and a second copy of the agent's logic in fork code.
- Treat "the agent connected" as Idle. It would say Idle while the printer prints or after it is unplugged, since that connect is a single request at startup.
- Leave it at "Not connected", which is what you asked me to fix.

Upstream wrote the block for exactly this purpose and disabled it only because their own Monitor tab does not show Moonraker printers. JusPrin's printer menu does, so switching it on is the smallest change that makes the state truthful.

content.text:
You are right, and my wording was wrong. Upstream's Device tab does show Moonraker printers. It shows them as the printer's own web page (Mainsail or Fluidd) loaded into a WebView from the preset's `print_host_webui`. That is a different thing from what the disabled block feeds.

What the block feeds is the native machine model: the `MachineObject` that knows whether the printer is connected and what it is printing. Upstream uses that model to drive the native Bambu-style status panel. For Moonraker, upstream leaves that model empty and lets the web page carry the status instead. That is what the "we don't use MonitorPanel for Moonraker printers yet" comment means: not that the tab is blank, but that the native panel is not the one on duty.

Two facts from upstream's current main support this:

- The block is still `#if 0` there today. It was added by SoftFever's "refactor" commit of 2026-01-27, and nothing else in upstream calls the status query or the websocket stream.
- Upstream recently added an opt-in setting, `use_printer_agents`, default off, that puts the native panel on the Device tab for non-Bambu printers. Even in that mode the stream stays disabled, which is why the comment says "yet". Our branch, based on v2.4.2, does not have that setting at all.

For JusPrin the web page is no help: the shell hides the tab strip, so neither Device tab is visible, and the printer menu wants a state word rather than a page. The only source for that word is the native model, and the only code that fills it for Moonraker is the block I enabled. The simulator has no web page either, which is fine, because nothing in the shell asks for one.
Explain the justification to me in plain English.

Here is the whole reasoning without the code names.

You asked for the printer menu to stop saying "Not connected" and show whether the fake printer is idle, printing, or offline. To say that, the app has to actually know the printer's state. It cannot guess; something inside the app has to be told, regularly, "the printer is printing" or "the printer stopped answering".

For Bambu printers, the app already gets told that. The printer streams its status over the network, and the app keeps a small record for each printer: the last time it heard from it, and what it was doing. The printer menu reads that record.

For Klipper printers, OrcaSlicer wrote the same kind of listener, one that asks the printer for its status and then keeps a live connection open for updates. Then they switched it off. Their reason was that their own Device tab shows a Klipper printer's web page instead, so their native status screen never needed the data. The listener is still in the code, unchanged, just disabled with a single switch.

JusPrin is in a different position. Its shell hides that Device tab entirely, and its printer menu wants a single word, not a web page. So the record has to be filled in, and the only code in the app that can fill it for a Klipper printer is that disabled listener. Turning the switch on is a two-line change to an upstream file. The alternatives were to write a second listener inside JusPrin's own code, which duplicates two hundred upstream lines, or to display "Idle" whenever the printer answered once at startup, which would lie the moment the printer started printing or was unplugged.

That is why the switch was flipped. I checked that upstream still has the switch in the same place, so a future rebase merges cleanly. If upstream ever turns it on themselves, the resolution is to take their version.

That dialog is JusPrin's, not OrcaSlicer's. Let me confirm what upstream does in the same situation before answering fully.

content.text:
No. That dialog exists only in JusPrin. The text is not anywhere in upstream OrcaSlicer; it was added by the fork commit that built the header's native print actions, before this session.

OrcaSlicer handles the same situation without a dialog. Its print button looks at the printer preset's host field. If a host is set, the button reads "Send" and sending goes through the upload dialog, the same one JusPrin uses. If no host is set, the button silently becomes "Export G-code" instead, and the send path is never offered. The underlying send routine also returns without a message if it finds no host.

JusPrin's header keeps one Print button whatever the printer, so instead of relabeling it, the shell checks the same host field and explains itself with that dialog when the field is empty. The condition behind it is identical to upstream's: Bambu network, or a non-empty print host. A Moonraker preset with a host set passes it in both programs, which is why the fake printer prints once its preset is selected.

What you hit was the preset, not the printer type: opening the saved 3mf switched you to the MyKlipper preset, which has no host, and both programs would have declined to send at that point. OrcaSlicer would have shown "Export G-code" on the button; JusPrin showed the dialog.

If we keep our fake printer's behavior exactly the same, then we don't have to change the upstream, right? The net will be able to send the prints to our fake printer, right? If not, tell me why not in plain English.

Right. Sending prints does not need the upstream change at all.

Printing worked before I touched any C++: both of my earlier verification runs used the untouched app, and the fake printer received the server check, the uploaded G-code, and the print-start command. That path only needs the preset to name a host, and the simulator to answer the four upload-related requests, which it did from the first version.

The upstream switch buys exactly one thing: the word in the printer menu. Without it the app never hears from a Klipper printer after the first hello, so it cannot know whether the printer is idle, printing, or gone. That is why, with only the fork-side change, the menu would say "Offline" forever, and with no change at all it says "Not connected". Sending is unaffected either way.

So the choice is yours:

- Keep the switch, and the menu shows Idle, Printing, and Offline for the fake printer and for any real Klipper printer.
- Drop it, and you get zero upstream footprint, prints still go to the fake printer, and the menu simply does not report state for non-Bambu printers.

If you want the second, I revert the two lines in the agent file and the shell change that depends on them, and leave the simulator, its tests, and the preset installer as they are.
what if we build a fake bambu printer? does it mean we can test all scenarios?

A fake Bambu printer would exercise the other half of the app, the half JusPrin's main users take, and the chip already reports state for Bambu printers, so no upstream switch would be needed. Whether it can test "all scenarios" depends on one hard constraint. Let me check it.

# Fake printer for testing without hardware

`fake_moonraker.py` is a stand-alone Moonraker (Klipper) printer written in
plain Python. JusPrin talks to it through the same network code it uses for a
real Klipper printer, so nothing in the C++ tree changes and the simulator
never conflicts with an upstream rebase. It answers the endpoints JusPrin
actually calls and adds a `/sim` control API so a person or an AI agent can
change the printer's state and read back what the app sent.

Moonraker was chosen over Bambu because Bambu printers need MQTT over TLS plus
FTP, while Moonraker is plain HTTP. Only the standard library is used, and
the tests run in about ten seconds.

## Run it

```bash
python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py
```

The server listens on `http://127.0.0.1:7125` and prints one line per request
the app makes, for example:

```
22:36:05 GET    /server/info                 server info (klippy_state=ready)
22:36:05 POST   /server/files/upload         upload plate_1.gcode (48211 bytes) {"plateindex": "1"}
22:36:05 POST   /printer/print/start         print start plate_1.gcode
```

Uploaded G-code is written to a folder under the temp directory (the path is
printed at startup; override with `--gcode-dir`). A started print heats up and
progresses to 100 % on its own over `--print-seconds` (default 60).

## Point JusPrin at it

JusPrin's shell hides the sidebar that opens the Physical Printer dialog, so
the simulator installs the printer preset for you. With JusPrin **closed**:

```bash
python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py --install-preset
```

This writes `user/default/machine/Fake Moonraker 0.4 nozzle.json` into the
JusPrin data directory (`~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2` on macOS,
`~/.config/JusPrin2` on Linux, `%APPDATA%\JusPrin2` on Windows) and selects it
as the current printer. The preset inherits the `MyKlipper 0.4 nozzle` system
preset from the Custom vendor; pass `--inherits` to use another installed
Klipper preset, and `--datadir` to target a different data directory.

After the next launch the header chip reads **Fake Moonraker · 0.4** (the chip
shows a preset's `printer_model`, which the installer sets). The chip's menu
has no preset picker, and JusPrin rewrites its config file on exit, so run the
installer only while the app is closed; otherwise the selection is lost.

## Manual test

1. Start the simulator.
2. Start JusPrin, load a model, slice it, and press **Print**. Accept the
   upload dialog.
3. Watch the simulator print the upload and the print start, then open
   `http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim` in a browser to see the print progress.

To put the printer into a particular state, POST JSON to `/sim`:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"state":"printing","filename":"benchy.gcode","progress":0.42}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"state":"paused"}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"klippy_state":"shutdown"}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"offline":true}'      # printer stops answering
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"reset":true}'
```

Accepted keys: `state` (`standby`, `printing`, `paused`, `complete`,
`cancelled`, `error`), `klippy_state` (`ready`, `startup`, `shutdown`,
`error`, `disconnected`), `filename`, `progress` (0 to 1), `extruder_temp`,
`extruder_target`, `bed_temp`, `bed_target`, `fan` (0 to 1), `homed`,
`message`, `offline`, `auto` (false freezes heating and progress), `lanes`
(replaces the AFC filament lanes), `clear_log`, `reset`. Unknown keys are
rejected so typos do not pass silently.

## Automated test (AI agent or script)

1. Start the simulator on a free port with a short print:
   `python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py --port 7125 --print-seconds 5 --quiet`
2. Copy the JusPrin data directory somewhere scratch, install the preset into
   it (`--install-preset --datadir <dir>`), and launch the app with
   `--datadir <dir> <model file>`. Set `OPENAI_API_KEY` to any value so the
   agent runtime does not open a Keychain prompt.
3. Drive the app, then assert on `GET /sim/log` (every request, oldest
   first, with `method`, `path`, and a one-line `summary`) and on `GET /sim`
   (state, temperatures, progress, uploaded `files`). `DELETE /sim/log`
   clears the log between steps. Fetch an uploaded file back with
   `GET /server/files/gcodes/<name>` to inspect the G-code the app produced.

On macOS the app can be driven without a screen by posting key events to its
process (this also works while the Mac is locked, where screenshot tools are
refused; mouse events are not delivered):

```bash
swiftc -O -o /tmp/mac_post_key tests/printer_sim/mac_post_key.swift
PID=$(pgrep -f "OrcaSlicer --datadir <dir>")
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 15 cmd            # Cmd+R: slice the plate
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 5 cmd shift       # Cmd+Shift+G: open the send dialog
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 48                # Tab: focus the Upload button
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 124               # Right: move to Upload and Print
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 49                # Space: press it
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim/log    # expect server info, upload, print start
```

This is the sequence that verified the whole path on 2026-09-07: the app
checked `/server/info`, uploaded the sliced cube (about 340 KB) and started
the print, and the simulator ran it to completion.

## Live state in the printer menu

Click the printer half of the header chip. The first row is the printer name
with its connection state, which comes from the simulator through JusPrin's
Moonraker printer agent:

| Simulator | Menu row |
|---|---|
| running, no print | **Idle** |
| running a print (started from JusPrin or `POST /sim {"state":"printing"}`) | **Printing** |
| stopped, or `POST /sim {"offline":true}` | **Offline** (about 30 seconds after the last status) |
| preset has no print host (for example after opening a project saved with another printer) | **Not connected** |

A few seconds after launch the agent connects (`GET /server/info`), reads the
initial status, and opens `ws://127.0.0.1:7125/websocket`, where the simulator
answers `server.connection.identify` and `printer.objects.subscribe` and then
pushes `notify_status_update` once a second. If the simulator goes away the
agent retries with growing delays (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... up to ten attempts);
restart the simulator within a few minutes and the row returns to Idle on its
own. After ten failed attempts, reselect the printer to reconnect.

One current limitation: the agent dials `https://` while the app setting
`enable_ssl_for_mqtt` is true, which is the default, and then fails with an
SSL connect error in the app log. Until that is fixed in the app, set it to
false in `JusPrin2.conf` before launching:

```json
"app": { "enable_ssl_for_mqtt": "false" }
```

The installer does not change this setting for you because it also governs
Bambu printers' LAN connections.

`test_fake_moonraker.py` shows every request shape:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/printer_sim -v
```

## What the app exercises

| JusPrin code | Endpoints |
|---|---|
| Print button (`src/slic3r/Utils/Moonraker.cpp`) | `GET /server/info`, `GET /server/files/roots`, `POST /server/files/upload`, `POST /printer/print/start` |
| Moonraker printer agent (`src/slic3r/Utils/MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp`) | `GET /server/info` on connect, `GET /printer/objects/query`, `GET /printer/objects/list`, `ws://…/websocket` (identify, subscribe, `notify_status_update`), `POST /printer/gcode/script`, `GET /server/database/item?namespace=lane_data` (AFC filament lanes) |

The G-code interpreter understands `G28`, `M104`/`M109`, `M140`/`M190`,
`M106`/`M107`, `SET_HEATER_TEMPERATURE`, `TURN_OFF_HEATERS`, `PAUSE`,
`RESUME`, `CANCEL_PRINT`, `SDCARD_PRINT_FILE`, `M112` and `FIRMWARE_RESTART`.
Everything else is accepted and logged.

## Known limits

- Opening a saved project switches to the printer stored in it. Import a
  model file instead, or pick the fake preset again under "Printer settings…".
- The websocket speaks only the methods the agent uses (identify, subscribe,
  query, server.info, printer.info, gcode.script) and pushes the full
  subscribed objects every second rather than diffs.
- No authentication and no Happy Hare `mmu` object.

## Test strategy

### Regression baselines and failure classification

Run the closest existing test and the broadest practical baseline before changing
an upstream-owned behavior. Record pre-existing failures by exact test name and
failure mode so later runs can distinguish a regression from inherited state.

When a broad suite fails, rerun the exact case independently before assigning a
cause. Record repeatable failures as regressions until disproved; record a
one-time timeout, deadlock, or infrastructure failure separately with the
isolated rerun result. A green focused suite does not erase a new repeatable
broad-suite failure.

### Contract tests

Test strong IDs, invalid/missing/stale identifiers, command errors, subscription lifetime, event coalescing, revision behavior, and fake-workspace history without linking the GUI. Test both successful and unsuccessful commands, and assert that reported results agree with authoritative state.

### Real-adapter application tests

A fake cannot validate `Plater`, `GLCanvas3D`, plate membership, `GUI_ObjectList` dependencies, event ordering, or Orca's undo stack. Add an application-level harness that loads deterministic project fixtures and covers:

- project-ready signaling rather than fixed event-loop delays;
- a dedicated application name and bundle identity so UI automation cannot target another Orca build;
- an isolated temporary configuration and repository-owned fixture;
- deterministic on-bed object placement, active tab, selection, and camera-visible state before reporting readiness;
- object and viewport selection in both directions;
- rename, duplicate, remove, plate switch, import, undo, and redo;
- committed native transform and exact-value transform;
- callback snapshots at the advertised revision;
- subscriber destruction;
- project replacement and session-ID invalidation;
- operations initiated outside the adapter.

The POC self-test is evidence and test-design input, not a production harness: its STL setup could not reproduce rename undo, and it intentionally terminated through `std::_Exit`.

### Shell end-to-end tests

Run the complete native application with a deterministic multi-plate project. Verify the visible real canvas, camera controls, selection, native gizmos, Slice, Check print, return to Prepare, undo/redo, object pane synchronization, Agent pane persistence, resize, maximize/restore, and the unchanged legacy layout when testing a compatibility mode.

Visual appearance alone is insufficient. Validate state from authoritative callbacks and pair visibility claims with screenshots or rendered evidence.

Use the harness to establish deterministic application state; use UI automation
for real pointer, keyboard, focus, and rendering checks rather than for fragile
startup setup. For canvas policy, inventory every overlay surface and verify
rendering and hit-testing separately. Compare a stock window with the product
policy, then exercise selection, orbit, pan, zoom, active gizmo input, slicing,
Preview, and restoration of the prior presentation state.

real Klipper printer, so tests exercise the app's real upload, print, and
status paths. It answers the endpoints JusPrin actually calls and adds a
`/sim` control API so a person or an AI agent can change the printer's state
and read back what the app sent.

Moonraker was chosen over Bambu because Bambu printers speak to a closed
network plugin over MQTT with TLS plus FTPS, while Moonraker is plain HTTP and
a websocket. Only the standard library is used, and the tests run in about
ten seconds:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/printer_sim -v
```

## What it simulates

| JusPrin code | What the simulator answers |
|---|---|
| Print button (`src/slic3r/Utils/Moonraker.cpp`) | `GET /server/info`, `GET /server/files/roots`, `POST /server/files/upload`, `POST /printer/print/start` |
| Moonraker printer agent (`src/slic3r/Utils/MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp`) | `GET /server/info` on connect, `GET /printer/objects/query`, `GET /printer/objects/list`, `ws://…/websocket` (`server.connection.identify`, `printer.objects.subscribe`, `notify_status_update` once a second), `POST /printer/gcode/script`, `GET /server/database/item?namespace=lane_data` (AFC filament lanes) |

A started print heats up and progresses to 100 % on its own over
`--print-seconds` (default 60). The G-code interpreter understands `G28`,
`M104`/`M109`, `M140`/`M190`, `M106`/`M107`, `SET_HEATER_TEMPERATURE`,
`TURN_OFF_HEATERS`, `PAUSE`, `RESUME`, `CANCEL_PRINT`, `SDCARD_PRINT_FILE`,
`M112` and `FIRMWARE_RESTART`; everything else is accepted and logged.

## Control API

Everything under `/sim` is the simulator's own, not Moonraker's.

| Request | Effect |
|---|---|
| `GET /sim` | Printer state (`state`, `klippy_state`, `filename`, `progress`, `extruder`, `heater_bed`, `fan`, `offline`), uploaded `files`, and the last 50 log entries |
| `POST /sim` with JSON | Change state; returns the new state. Unknown keys are rejected so typos do not pass silently |
| `GET /sim/log` | Every request the app made, oldest first: `time`, `method`, `path`, one-line `summary` |
| `DELETE /sim/log` | Clear the log between steps |
| `GET /server/files/gcodes/<name>` | Download a file the app uploaded |

Keys accepted by `POST /sim`: `state` (`standby`, `printing`, `paused`,
`complete`, `cancelled`, `error`), `klippy_state` (`ready`, `startup`,
`shutdown`, `error`, `disconnected`), `filename`, `progress` (0 to 1),
`extruder_temp`, `extruder_target`, `bed_temp`, `bed_target`, `fan` (0 to 1),
`homed`, `message`, `offline` (true makes the printer stop answering, the
websocket included), `auto` (false freezes heating and progress), `lanes`
(replaces the AFC filament lanes), `clear_log`, `reset`.

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"state":"printing","filename":"benchy.gcode","progress":0.42}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"state":"paused"}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"klippy_state":"shutdown"}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"offline":true}'
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"reset":true}'
```

## What JusPrin shows

Open the printer half of the header chip. The first row of its menu is the
printer name with the connection state, computed by
`SetupCommands::printer_connection` from the status the agent receives:

| Simulator | Menu row |
|---|---|
| running, no print | **Idle** |
| running a print, started from JusPrin or with `POST /sim {"state":"printing"}` | **Printing** |
| stopped, or `POST /sim {"offline":true}` | **Offline**, about 30 seconds after the last status |
| the selected preset has no print host | **Not connected** |

The chip itself reads **Fake Moonraker · 0.4**. A few seconds after launch the
agent connects, reads the initial status, and opens the websocket. If the
simulator goes away the agent retries with growing delays (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, up
to ten attempts); restart the simulator within a few minutes and the row
returns to Idle on its own. After ten failed attempts, reselect the printer.

## Setup, once

JusPrin's shell hides the dialog that would let you type a print host, so the
simulator installs the printer preset. With JusPrin **closed**:

```bash
python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py --install-preset
```

This writes `user/default/machine/Fake Moonraker 0.4 nozzle.json` into the
JusPrin data directory (`~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2` on macOS,
`~/.config/JusPrin2` on Linux, `%APPDATA%\JusPrin2` on Windows) and selects it
as the current printer. The preset inherits the `MyKlipper 0.4 nozzle` system
preset from the Custom vendor (`--inherits` picks another installed Klipper
preset, `--datadir` another data directory, `--port` another port). JusPrin
rewrites its config on exit and the chip's menu has no preset picker, so an
installer run while the app is open is lost.

One current limitation: the agent dials `https://` while the app setting
`enable_ssl_for_mqtt` is true, which is the default, and then fails with an
SSL connect error in the app log. Until that is fixed in the app, set it to
false in `JusPrin2.conf` (with the app closed):

```bash
python3 -c "import json,os; p=os.path.expanduser('~/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/JusPrin2.conf'); c=json.load(open(p)); c.setdefault('app',{})['enable_ssl_for_mqtt']='false'; json.dump(c,open(p,'w'),indent='\t',ensure_ascii=False)"
```

The installer does not change this setting itself because it also governs
Bambu printers' LAN connections.

## Manual test: printer status

1. Start the simulator and leave the terminal open:
   `python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py`
2. Start JusPrin. Within a few seconds the simulator prints `server info`,
   `status query`, `websocket connected`, and `subscribe: …`.
3. Click the printer half of the chip. The first row reads **Fake Moonraker ·
   Idle**. Click elsewhere to close the menu.
4. In another terminal: `curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"state":"printing","filename":"benchy.gcode","progress":0.4}'`.
   Reopen the menu: **Printing**.
5. `curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim -d '{"state":"complete"}'`.
   Reopen the menu: **Idle**.
6. Press Ctrl+C in the simulator's terminal. Wait 30 seconds, reopen the menu:
   **Offline**.
7. Start the simulator again. Within about a minute the menu is back to
   **Idle**, and the simulator has printed a new `websocket connected` line.

## Manual test: sending a print

1. With the simulator running, import a model file into JusPrin (drag an STL
   in, or use the Import button). Do not open a saved 3mf project: a project
   carries its own printer preset and switches away from the fake printer.
2. Press **Slice**, then **Print**, then **Upload and Print** in the dialog.
3. The simulator prints four lines: storage roots, server info, the upload
   with its byte count, and the print start. Reopen the chip menu:
   **Printing**. `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7125/sim` shows the filename and
   the progress climbing to 1.0 over a minute, after which the menu says
   **Idle** again.

1. Start the simulator on a free port with a short print, quiet:
   `python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py --port 7135 --print-seconds 5 --quiet &`
2. Copy the JusPrin data directory to a scratch folder, clear
   `recent_projects` in its `JusPrin2.conf`, set `enable_ssl_for_mqtt` to
   `"false"` (see above), and install the preset into it:
   `python3 tests/printer_sim/fake_moonraker.py --install-preset --datadir <dir> --port 7135`
3. Launch the built app against it with a model, and give the agent runtime a
   dummy key so it does not open a Keychain prompt:
   `OPENAI_API_KEY=x <app>/Contents/MacOS/OrcaSlicer --datadir <dir> tests/data/20mm_cube.obj &`
4. Connection check: within about 10 seconds `GET /sim/log` contains
   `/server/info`, `/printer/objects/query`, `websocket connected`, and a
   `subscribe:` entry. The app's own log under `<dir>/log/` contains
   `MoonrakerPrinterAgent: connect_printer completed`.
5. Print check: slice and send (see below), then assert that `GET /sim/log`
   ends with `/server/files/upload` and `/printer/print/start`, and that
   `GET /sim` reports `"state": "printing"` with the uploaded filename. Fetch
   the file back with `GET /server/files/gcodes/<name>` to inspect the
   G-code the app produced.
6. State checks: `POST /sim` with `offline`, `state`, temperatures, or
   progress, and read the app's reaction from its log or from screenshots of
   the chip menu (the desktop-control tools can open it with a click on the
   printer half of the chip once the app is frontmost).

On macOS the app can be driven without a screen by posting key events to its
process. This also works while the Mac is locked, where screenshot tools are
refused; mouse events are not delivered that way:

```bash
swiftc -O -o /tmp/mac_post_key tests/printer_sim/mac_post_key.swift
PID=$(pgrep -f "OrcaSlicer --datadir <dir>")

/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 5 cmd shift       # Cmd+Shift+G: open the send dialog
sleep 4
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 48                # Tab: focus the Upload button
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 124               # Right: move to Upload and Print
/tmp/mac_post_key $PID 49                # Space: press it
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:7135/sim/log    # expect server info, upload, print start
```

This is the sequence that verified the whole path on 2026-09-07 and
2026-09-08: the app checked `/server/info`, uploaded the sliced cube (about
340 KB), started the print, and the chip menu showed Idle, Printing, and
Offline as the simulator's state changed.

## Known limits

- Opening a saved project switches to the printer stored in it. Import a
  model file instead, or pick the fake preset again under "Printer settings…".
- The websocket speaks only the methods the agent uses and pushes the full
  subscribed objects every second rather than diffs.
- No authentication and no Happy Hare `mmu` object.

websocket stream (identify, subscribe, notify_status_update). A started
print heats up and progresses on its own; a small G-code interpreter
handles the commands the agent sends. A /sim control API sets the
printer's state (printing, paused, offline, temperatures, Klipper down)
and returns a log of every request the app made, which is what a person
or an AI agent asserts on.

JusPrin's shell hides the dialog that sets a print host, so
--install-preset writes a user printer preset pointing at the simulator
(printer_model "Fake Moonraker", so the header chip names it) and selects
it in the app config. It copies the vendor's version string because a
preset whose version does not parse is silently skipped at load.

mac_post_key.swift posts key events to the app's process so an agent can
slice and press Print without a screen; this also works while the Mac is
locked, where screenshot tools are refused.

23 unit tests drive the simulator with the exact request shapes from
Moonraker.cpp and MoonrakerPrinterAgent.cpp. Verified against the built
app twice: it uploaded the sliced cube and started the print, and the
simulator ran it to completion. The README carries the manual and the
agent procedures, and engineering-method.md points at it.
